title: El verbo 'sein' (ser/estar) / The verb 'sein' (to be)
bridge: In Spanish we have two verbs for 'ser' and 'estar', and we use them depending on whether something is permanent (ser) or temporary (estar). In German there is only one verb for both: 'sein'. The good news is that you don't have to worry about that distinction: 'Ich bin müde' works for both 'Soy cansado' and 'Estoy cansado' (in this case, it's always said 'estoy cansado', but the idea is that 'sein' covers both cases). The real difficulty is that 'sein' is an irregular verb and changes a lot depending on the person.
rule: The verb 'sein' in the present tense: ich bin (I am), du bist (you are), er/sie/es ist (he/she/it is), wir sind (we are), ihr seid (you all are), sie/Sie sind (they are / you are, formal). To negate, add 'nicht' after the verb: 'Ich bin nicht müde' (I am not tired). To ask a question, the verb comes first: 'Bist du müde?' (Are you tired?).

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, the verb can sometimes be implied in colloquial phrases, but in German 'sein' is mandatory in every sentence, just like in correct Spanish ('Estoy cansado', not 'Yo cansado'). Never omit 'bin/bist/ist/sind/seid'.

examples.note: We use 'bin' only with 'ich'.
We use 'ist' for the third person singular.
'Nicht' is placed after the conjugated verb.
We invert the subject and verb to form questions, just like in Spanish.

title: Los artículos y el género: der, die, das / Articles and gender: der, die, das
bridge: In Spanish, nouns have two genders (masculine and feminine), and you can usually recognize them by their endings (-o, -a). In German, there are THREE genders: masculine (der), feminine (die), and neuter (das). The hardest part for Spanish speakers is that the gender in German rarely matches the gender in Spanish, and you can't always guess it by the word's ending. For example, 'das Mädchen' (the girl) is neuter, not feminine, because all words ending in '-chen' are neuter in German, without exception. The best advice is to learn each noun together with its article, as if they were a single word.
rule: Definite articles (the) in singular: der (masculine, e.g. der Mann = the man), die (feminine, e.g. die Frau = the woman), das (neuter, e.g. das Kind = the child). In plural, all three genders use 'die': die Männer, die Frauen, die Kinder. Some useful clues (not absolute rules): words ending in '-chen' or '-lein' are always neuter (das Mädchen); those ending in '-heit', '-keit', '-ung', '-schaft' are always feminine (die Freiheit, die Zeitung); days, months, and cardinal points are usually masculine (der Montag, der Winter).

common_error.wrong: die Mädchen (thinking that 'girl' must be feminine, as in Spanish)
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, grammatical gender usually matches meaning (girl = feminine), but in German, gender is a grammatical category independent of meaning. All words ending in '-chen' are neuter by rule, regardless of what they refer to.

examples.note: In Spanish 'mesa' is feminine, in German 'Tisch' is masculine: genders do not match.
In Spanish 'sol' is masculine, in German 'Sonne' is feminine.
Neuter has no direct equivalent in Spanish; you simply have to memorize it.
In plural, all three genders share the same article: 'die'.

title: Sein – Verbo ser/estar
bridge: In German, the verb 'sein' covers both 'ser' and 'estar', just like in Spanish, but its conjugation is highly irregular. Unlike Spanish, German does not omit the subject: 'ich', 'du', 'er', etc., must always appear. Additionally, German does not use the verb 'sein' for temporary states like 'estoy cansado' (ich bin müde), but it does distinguish between 'wohnen' (to live) and 'sein' (to be) in location contexts.
rule: The verb 'sein' is the equivalent of both 'ser' and 'estar'. It is conjugated irregularly in the present tense: ich bin (I am), du bist (you are), er/sie/es ist (he/she/it is), wir sind (we are), ihr seid (you all are), sie/Sie sind (they are / you are formal). It is used for: identity (Ich bin Ana), profession (Er ist Arzt), origin (Wir sind aus Spanien), location (Die Katze ist im Haus), physical and emotional states (Ich bin müde), and permanent characteristics (Das Auto ist rot). Unlike Spanish, there is no distinction between 'ser' and 'estar'; context and adjectives determine the nuance. Remember that the subject is always present, even if the context makes it clear.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers tend to translate 'yo soy contento' literally, omitting the subject. In German, the subject is mandatory: 'ich' cannot be omitted. Additionally, 'contento' as a temporary emotional state is expressed with 'glücklich' or 'froh', not with 'zufrieden' (which means rather 'satisfied'). The structure is 'pronoun + bin + adjective', without an indefinite article.

examples.note: Use 'bin' for the first person; do not say 'yo soy' omitting the subject.
'Du' is informal singular; for respect, use 'Sie sind'.
Professions are used without an article in the singular.
'Krank' is a temporary state; 'sein' is used instead of 'estar' as in Spanish.
'Zufrieden' is used for satisfaction, not for momentary happiness.
'Glücklich' can refer to a state or trait; here it can mean 'she is happy'.
For origin, use 'aus' + country, not 'de' as in Spanish.

examples.original: Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.
examples.phonetic: das buːx ɪst aʊf deːm tɪʃ
examples.translation: The book is on the table.
examples.note: 'Auf' indicates a surface; remember 'sein' is used for location.

examples.translation: They are at the department store.
examples.note: The contraction 'im' (in + dem) is common; it means 'in the'.

title: Der bestimmte und unbestimmte Artikel (Definite and indefinite articles)
bridge: In Spanish, we say 'el', 'la', 'los', 'las' for definite articles, and 'un', 'una', 'unos', 'unas' for indefinite ones. In German, the article changes not only by gender (masculine, feminine, neuter) but also by case (nominative, accusative, dative, genitive). Unlike Spanish, German has a neuter article 'das' and uses a case system that modifies articles according to their function in the sentence, something that does not exist in Spanish. Additionally, indefinite articles have no plural form in German.
rule: In German, articles agree with gender (maskulin, feminin, neutral), number (singular, plural), and case (Nominativ, Akkusativ, Dativ, Genitiv). For A1, it is essential to master the nominative and accusative cases. In nominative: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter), die (plural) for definite articles; ein (masculine), eine (feminine), ein (neuter) for indefinite articles (no plural). In accusative, the only change is in masculine: der becomes den, and ein becomes einen. The negative indefinite article is formed with 'kein' (for masculine/neuter) and 'keine' (for feminine). Learn to identify the gender of nouns (for example, those ending in -ung, -heit, -keit are usually feminine; those ending in -er are usually masculine) and memorize the articles from the beginning, as they are fundamental for case and agreement.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'un hermano' uses an indefinite article that does not change with the verb 'tener' (to have). In German, the verb 'haben' (to have) requires the accusative case, and the masculine indefinite article 'ein' changes to 'einen'. That is why it is common to forget the ending '-en'. To avoid this, remember that in accusative only the masculine changes to 'den' and 'einen'.

examples.note: Here 'der' is masculine in nominative (subject).
'Die' is used for singular feminine in nominative.
'Das' is the neuter article.
The plural 'die' is used for all genders.
'Ein' for masculine, like 'un' in Spanish.
The ending '-e' indicates feminine.
For neuter, 'ein' is also used without an ending.
The masculine 'der' changes to 'den' in accusative (direct object).
The indefinite 'ein' becomes 'einen' for masculine accusative.
Feminine and plural do not change in accusative.
The neuter article remains 'das' in accusative.

title: Geschlecht und Zahl der Nomen / Gender and number of nouns
bridge: In Spanish, nouns typically have masculine or feminine gender, often deduced from their endings (-o/-a). In German, there are three genders: masculine, feminine, and neuter, and the gender is not always clear. Additionally, the article (der/die/das) changes with gender, and in the plural, all genders use 'die'. Unlike Spanish, the plural in German has various forms (e.g., adding -e, -er, -n, or no change), which requires memorization.
rule: In German, every noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (der), feminine (die), or neuter (das). The definite article in singular is: der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter). In the plural, the article is always 'die', regardless of gender. For A1 learners, it is essential to learn each noun with its article. There are some clues: nouns ending in -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft are usually feminine (die Zeitung, die Freiheit). Nouns ending in -er, -en, -el are often masculine or neuter (der Lehrer, der Kuchen). Diminutives with -chen or -lein are neuter (das Mädchen). The plural is formed in various ways: adding -e (der Tisch -> die Tische), -er (das Kind -> die Kinder), -n/-en (die Frau -> die Frauen), -s (das Auto -> die Autos), or no change (das Mädchen -> die Mädchen). Some nouns change the vowel (der Vater -> die Väter). For A1 learners, it is recommended to learn the plural form along with the noun, for example, 'der Mann, die Männer'.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, 'mujer' is feminine and we use 'la'. In German, 'Frau' is also feminine, but the article is 'die', not 'der'. The error occurs because the student confuses 'der' (masculine) with 'la' (feminine) due to the influence of Spanish. To avoid this, it is crucial to associate each noun with its article from the beginning, for example, learning 'die Frau' as a single unit.

levels.label: Bestimmter Artikel im Singular (Artículo definido en singular)

examples.note: Masculine: der. Remember that in Spanish 'mesa' is feminine, but in German it is masculine. Learn the word with its article.
Feminine: die. Many words ending in -e are feminine, but not always.
Neuter: das. In Spanish 'libro' is masculine, but in German it is neuter. There is no fixed rule; memorize.
Many masculine nouns form the plural by adding -e.
Feminine nouns often add -n or -en.
Some neuter nouns add -er. Note that the article in plural is always 'die'.
Vowel change (Umlaut) and ending -er. A common exception.
Despite referring to a girl (feminine), it is grammatically neuter due to the suffix -chen.
Foreign loanwords often add -s in plural.

title: Regelmäßige Verben im Präsens / Regular verbs in the present tense
bridge: In German, regular verbs in the present tense are conjugated in a way very similar to Spanish: you remove the -en ending from the infinitive and add an ending according to the person. However, there are two key differences: there is no progressive form (like 'estoy hablando'), and the verb always occupies the second position in the sentence, even in questions. Additionally, pay attention to the forms for 'du' and 'ihr', which do not have a direct equivalent in Spanish (they correspond to 'tú/vosotros' and 'vosotros', respectively).
rule: In German, regular verbs in the present tense are conjugated as follows: take the infinitive (e.g., 'machen' - to do), remove the -en ending (leaving 'mach-'), and add the ending corresponding to each person: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir -en, ihr -t, sie/Sie -en. Examples with 'machen': ich mache, du machst, er macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie machen. Exception: if the stem ends in -t or -d (like in 'arbeiten'), an 'e' is added before the -st and -t endings to facilitate pronunciation: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. In affirmative sentences, the conjugated verb goes in second position. In questions, it goes in first position. Auxiliaries are not used to form the present continuous; the simple present covers both uses.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers often add an extra 's' in the first person singular (I) because in Spanish we say 'hago', not 'hagost'. In German, the correct ending for 'ich' is just '-e'. Avoid transferring Spanish verb endings directly to German.

examples.note: Observe the '-e' ending for 'ich'.
The '-st' ending is used only with 'du'.
For 'er/sie/es', use '-t' (replaces the infinitive ending).
'Wir' uses the same ending as the infinitive: '-en'.
An 'e' is added before '-st' because the stem ends in 't'.
Same with stems ending in 'd': 'red-e-t' instead of 'red-t'.
Be careful: 'ihr' means 'vosotros', and it uses '-t', but it is sometimes confused with the third person singular.

examples.translation: They are looking for a hotel.
examples.note: The form 'sie' (they) is the same as 'wir' and 'Sie' (formal you).
In questions, the verb comes first. You do not need 'do/does' as in English, and German does not use question marks.
Negation with 'nicht' comes after the verb and usually at the end if there is no specific complement.
In German, the conjugated verb remains in second position even with negation.
The question form for 'ihr' is the same as the affirmative, only the word order changes.

translations.en: Regular verbs in the present tense

title: Negación: nicht / kein
bridge: In Spanish, negation is usually simple: we add 'no' before the verb. In German, there are two main words for negation: 'nicht' and 'kein'. 'Nicht' is used to negate verbs, adjectives, or entire phrases, while 'kein' is used to negate nouns with indefinite articles or no article. The position of 'nicht' in the German sentence can also be confusing for Spanish speakers, as it does not always go before the verb, but rather at the end or before the word being negated.
rule:
To negate in German at A1 level, the main words used are 'nicht' and 'kein'. 

**Uses of 'nicht':** 
- To negate verbs: 'Ich komme nicht.' (I am not coming.) 
- To negate adjectives or adverbs: 'Das ist nicht gut.' (That is not good.) 
- To negate nouns with definite articles or possessives: 'Das ist nicht mein Buch.' (That is not my book.) 
- To negate an entire phrase: 'Er arbeitet nicht.' (He does not work.) 

**Position of 'nicht':** It generally goes at the end of the sentence if it negates the main verb, or immediately before the word being negated (adjective, adverb, etc.). 

**Uses of 'kein':** 
- Used to negate nouns that in affirmative sentences would take 'ein/eine' or no article (countable or uncountable nouns). 
- It is declined like the indefinite article: 'kein' (masculine/neuter nominative), 'keine' (feminine nominative or plural), 'keinen' (masculine accusative), etc. 
- Examples: 'Ich habe kein Geld.' (I have no money.) / 'Ich habe keine Zeit.' (I have no time.) 

**Comparison with Spanish:** In Spanish, 'no' is always used before the verb, and the noun does not change. In German, when negating a noun with 'kein', the article disappears or changes form, which requires attention. Additionally, in Spanish double negation is common and accepted, but in German only one negation is used at a time. 

**Important exception:** In answering a question with 'doch' (yes, contrary to what was said), neither 'nicht' nor 'kein' is used, but rather 'doch'.

concept_examples.translation: I do not have a car.

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we say 'no tengo tiempo' with the adverb 'no' before the verb. In German, when negating a noun without a definite article or with an indefinite article, 'kein/e' must be used instead of 'nicht'. 'Zeit' (time) is a feminine uncountable noun, so 'keine' is used. To avoid this mistake, ask yourself: what am I negating? If it is a noun, use 'kein' (with its declension); if it is a verb, adjective, or adverb, use 'nicht'.

examples.note: Here 'nicht' negates the adjective 'müde' (tired). It goes before the adjective.
When negating the verb, 'nicht' goes at the end of the sentence.
'nicht' is used with nouns that have a possessive or definite article.
'Geld' is neuter and without an article, so 'kein' (nominative/accusative neuter) is used.
In the plural, 'kein' becomes 'keine'.

examples.original: Hast du einen Bruder? – Nein, ich habe keinen Bruder.
examples.phonetic: [hast duː ˈaɪ̯nən ˈbʁuːdɐ | naɪ̯n, ɪç ˈhaːbə ˈkaɪ̯nən ˈbʁuːdɐ]
examples.translation: Do you have a brother? – No, I do not have a brother.
examples.note: In the accusative masculine, 'kein' becomes 'keinen'.

examples.translation: I do not have much time.
examples.note: Here 'nicht' negates the quantity 'viel' (much), not the noun, so 'nicht' is used.
We use 'keine' because we are directly negating the noun 'Zeit'.

examples.original: Das ist nicht mein Glas. Das ist dein Glas.
examples.phonetic: [das ɪst nɪçt maɪ̯n glaːs | das ɪst daɪ̯n glaːs]
examples.translation: That is not my glass. That is your glass.
examples.note: With a possessive article ('mein'), 'nicht' is used.

title: Fragen stellen / Basic questions
bridge: In Spanish, yes/no questions are formed simply with intonation (¿Hablas español?). In German, in addition to intonation, the conjugated verb is placed at the beginning. For questions with interrogatives (what, who, where...), the interrogative word (W-Frage) goes first, followed by the verb. Thus, the order is reversed: subject and verb are swapped in direct questions. Pay attention to German interrogatives: "wo" (where) may look like "was" (what), don't confuse them!
rule:
In German, there are two types of questions: yes/no questions (Ja/Nein-Fragen) and questions with interrogatives (W-Fragen).

1. **Ja/Nein-Fragen**: The conjugated verb goes at the beginning of the sentence, followed by the subject. The intonation rises at the end. For example: "Kommst du?" (Are you coming?), "Sprichst du Spanisch?" (Do you speak Spanish?).

2. **W-Fragen**: The interrogative word (warum, wann, woher, etc.) goes first, followed by the conjugated verb and then the subject. The most common interrogatives at A1 level are:
   - **wer** (who) - for people
   - **was** (what) - for things
   - **wo** (where) - for place
   - **woher** (where from) - for origin
   - **wohin** (where to) - for direction
   - **wann** (when) - for time
   - **warum** (why) - for reason
   - **wie** (how) - for manner

**Exception**: The interrogative "wer" (who) requires the verb to be conjugated in the third person singular, regardless of whom it refers to. For example: "Wer bist du?" (Who are you?) is correct; "wer" always takes singular conjugation: "Wer bist du?" is correct (bist = second person singular). There is no exception here.

**Use of "wie" with "viel" and "viele"**: "Wie viel" (how much?) for uncountable nouns, "wie viele" (how many?) for countable nouns. This is not covered in depth at A1, but it's useful to know.

**Intonation**: In yes/no questions, the intonation rises at the end; in W-Fragen, the intonation falls.

**Order in questions with complements**: When there is a prepositional complement, the verb+subject order is maintained. Example: "Woher kommst du?" (Where do you come from? literally: from where do you come?).

**Comparison with Spanish**: In Spanish, questions are formed with optional inversion or just intonation, and sometimes the interrogative is used at the beginning. In German, inversion is mandatory.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, a yes/no question can be formed simply by changing the intonation of a declarative sentence (¿Tú hablas español?). In German, this type of question requires mandatory inversion of the verb and subject: the conjugated verb must come at the beginning. Maintaining the declarative order with only intonation sounds very informal and is not correct in standard German. Remember that in Ja/Nein-Fragen, the verb always occupies the first position.

examples.note: The verb 'sein' (to be) is conjugated in the second person singular 'bist' and goes at the beginning. In Spanish, you can ask with just intonation, but in German the verb-subject order is mandatory.
Verb 'kommen' conjugated in second person singular 'kommst' at the beginning. The preposition 'aus' indicates origin, just like 'de' in Spanish.
The verb 'haben' in second person 'hast' comes at the beginning. 'Geschwister' is a plural meaning 'siblings' in a generic sense (does not specify gender).

levels.label: W-Fragen: wer, was, wo
levels.translation: Questions with interrogatives: who, what, where

examples.note: 'Wer' (who) refers to the identity of a person. The verb is conjugated in second person singular after 'wer', maintaining the order wer + verb + subject.
'Was' (what) asks about things or concepts. Verb 'ist' in third person singular and the subject 'das' (that) comes after. This is a very common question.
'Wo' (where) asks about place. The verb 'wohnen' in second person singular 'wohnst' comes after the interrogative.
'Woher' (where from) asks about origin. Do not confuse with 'wo': 'woher' indicates origin, while 'wo' indicates location.
'Wann' (when) asks about time. Verb 'haben' in second person singular 'hast' after the interrogative. The accusative case is used (days, dates).

'Warum' (why) asks about reason. Remember that in German there is no difference in writing between 'why' and 'because', but in pronunciation and sentence order it is distinguished: 'warum' starts the question; 'weil' introduces a subordinate clause.

examples.translation: What's your name? (literally: how are you called?)
examples.note: 'Wie' (how) is essential for introducing yourself. The verb 'heißen' (to be called) is conjugated in second person singular 'heißt'. In Spanish we use the verb 'llamarse'.

examples.translation: What time is it? (literally: how late is it?)
examples.note: Fixed expression to ask for the time. 'Wie spät' literally means 'how late'. In German this structure is used instead of '¿qué hora es?'.

title: Zahlen 1-100 / Numbers from 1 to 100
bridge: In Spanish, numbers are formed in a relatively simple way: after 15, we simply say 'dieciséis', 'diecisiete', etc. In German, you need to pay attention to the inversion: for numbers from 21 to 99, the unit is said first, followed by the tens, joined with 'und' (and), for example, 'einundzwanzig' (21) literally means 'one and twenty'. Additionally, unlike Spanish, numbers in German can act as nouns and are then written with a capital letter (die Eins, die Zwei).
rule: In German, numbers from 1 to 12 have their own names (eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf). From 13 to 19, they are formed by adding '-zehn' to the root: dreizehn (13), vierzehn, fünfzehn, sechzehn (be careful with the loss of the 's'), siebzehn (loses 'en'), achtzehn, neunzehn. The tens (20, 30, ... 90) are formed with the root plus '-zig' (zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig). For compound numbers from 21 to 99, the unit is said first, followed by 'und' and then the tens: einundzwanzig (21), zweiunddreißig (32). The number 100 is 'hundert'. Numbers are written as one word. When reading them, they are pronounced in one go.

concept_examples.text: Wir treffen uns um dreißig Minuten.
concept_examples.phonetic: viːɐ̯ ˈtʁɛfən ʊns ʊm ˈdʁaɪ̯sɪç miˈnuːtən

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we say the tens first and then the unit (veintiuno), but in German the order is reversed: first the unit, then 'und', and then the tens. Also remember that 'ein' is used without an 's' in compounds, and that 'und' is not used between units if the number is just a ten or a unit.

examples.note: Memorize the first numbers. Note that 'eins' becomes 'ein' when used before a noun.
Pronunciation: 'sechs' is pronounced like 'zex' (with a voiced 's' at the beginning).
The 'ch' in 'acht' is pronounced like a soft 'j', not like a 'k'.
Although 'elf' and 'zwölf' seem irregular, they are very common, so get used to them.
Tens end in '-zig' except 'dreißig', which uses 'ß' (ess-zett).
Remember: say the unit first (ein) + und + tens (zwanzig).
Notice the inversion and that 'sechs' sometimes loses the 's' in compounds, but here it is kept.
It is not said as 'einhundert' for 100, but it can be used for emphasis.
To say age in German, the verb 'sein' (to be) is used, not 'haben' (to have). This is an important contrast with Spanish.
Practice with prices: it is common to use numbers in shops.
It is a high number to practice inversion and the pronunciation of 'und'.

title: Adjektive und ihre Endungen / Adjective endings and agreement
bridge: In Spanish, adjectives change only in gender and number (e.g., 'bueno' → 'buena', 'buenos'). In German, in addition to gender and number, they also depend on the case (nominative, accusative, dative, genitive) and whether they are preceded by a definite, indefinite, or no article. As a Spanish speaker, you will be familiar with the idea of agreement, but you will need to learn to observe the adjective ending based on the preceding article. A typical mistake is to always use the base form of the adjective without adding the correct ending.
rule:
German adjectives in attributive function (before the noun) receive an ending that depends on three factors: (1) the gender of the noun (masculine, feminine, neuter), (2) the number (singular or plural), and (3) the case (nominative for the subject, accusative for the direct object, dative for the indirect object, genitive for possession). At A1 level, we focus on nominative and accusative.

With definite articles (der, die, das), the endings are: in nominative: der kleine Mann, die kleine Frau, das kleine Kind; in accusative: den kleinen Mann, die kleine Frau, das kleine Kind. The typical ending is -e in nominative singular and -en in the rest (except neuter and feminine in nominative/accusative, which remain -e).

With indefinite articles (ein, eine, ein): masculine nominative: ein kleiner Mann, accusative: einen kleinen Mann; feminine: eine kleine Frau (nominative and accusative); neuter: ein kleines Kind (nominative and accusative). Note that the ending reflects the gender of the noun when the article does not clearly show it.

Without an article (e.g., in plural or with uncountable nouns): the adjective takes the ending of the definite article: kleine Kinder, teurer Wein. In singular without an article, the strong ending is also used: guter Kaffee, gute Milch, gutes Bier.

For A1, memorize the patterns with the most common adjectives: groß, klein, gut, neu, schön, alt, jung, teuer, billig, hoch. Remember that 'hoch' drops the 'c' when declined: ein hoher Berg. The adjective 'teuer' drops the 'e' in the declined form: ein teures Auto.

common_error.correct_alt: Ich habe ein Haus, das groß ist.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we say 'tengo una casa grande' without changing the adjective based on the article. In German, with the neuter indefinite article ('ein'), the adjective needs the ending -es to mark the neuter gender in nominative/accusative. Forgetting the ending is very common. Think: the article 'ein' does not clearly show the gender (it can be masculine or neuter), so the adjective ending compensates for that information. Memorize: ein + adjective + -es for neuter, -en for masculine accusative, -e for feminine.

examples.note: Here 'groß' is an attribute of the subject, but after 'ist' the base form without ending is used. It is not declined.
Same case: predicative adjective, no ending.
Here 'kleine' takes -e because it is an attribute before the neuter noun with the definite article 'das' in nominative.

examples.translation: I am buying a new computer.
examples.note: In masculine accusative, the article becomes 'einen' and the adjective takes -en.
Feminine: both nominative and accusative use 'eine' + adjective with -e.

examples.translation: We are looking for a cheap hotel.
examples.note: Neuter: 'ein' + adjective with -es. Note that 'billig' remains in its base form and only the ending is added.
Without an article, the adjective takes the strong ending of the definite article: masculine nominative → -er.
Feminine without an article: -e (same as with indefinite article).
Neuter without an article: -es. Remember that in plural without an article, -e is used: 'große Fenster'.

title: Possessivartikel / Possessives
bridge: In Spanish we use 'mi', 'tu', 'su', etc. which agree in number with the noun (mi libro, mis libros). In German, the possessives (mein, dein, sein, etc.) also agree in gender, number, and case with the noun they accompany. A key point is that in German there is no single form for 'su': it depends on who owns it (his: sein, hers: ihr, theirs: ihr, formal you: Ihr). Additionally, German possessives have endings that change depending on the noun's gender: mein Vater (masculine), meine Mutter (feminine), mein Kind (neuter). Be careful: in Spanish 'su' is ambiguous, but in German you must choose the correct form based on the owner.
rule: German possessives (Possessivartikel) agree with the noun they modify in gender (masculine, feminine, neuter), number (singular/plural), and case (nominative, accusative, dative, genitive). At A1 level, we focus on nominative and accusative cases. The basic forms in nominative are: mein (my, masculine/neuter), meine (my, feminine/plural), dein (your, masculine/neuter), deine (your, feminine/plural), sein (his), seine (hers/plural), ihr (her), ihre (her/plural), unser (our), unsere (our/plural), euer (your), eure (your/plural), ihr/Ihr (their/your formal). In accusative, the masculine changes: meinen, deinen, seinen, ihren, unseren, euren (e.g. Ich sehe meinen Vater). Feminine and neuter do not change in accusative. Remember that the possessive comes before the noun and replaces the article. For A1, it is essential to memorize the nominative and accusative forms with the genders.

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish the possessive 'tu' does not change with the case (quiero a tu hermano). In German, when the noun is masculine and in accusative (direct object), the possessive must have the ending '-en': deinen. Thus, 'dein' becomes 'deinen' before a masculine noun in accusative. Remember: for masculine in accusative, add '-en'.

examples.note: For masculine nouns (der Tisch), we use 'mein' without an ending.
For feminine nouns (die Tasche), we add '-e' to 'dein': deine.
For neuter nouns (das Kind), we use 'mein' without an ending, just like masculine.
'Sein' is used when the owner is masculine (he).
'Ihr' is used when the owner is feminine (she).
With feminine nouns, we add '-e' to 'sein': seine.
'Unser' is used for 'our' with masculine or neuter nouns.
'Eure' is the form for 'your' (plural) with plural nouns.
For 'their', we use 'ihr' (lowercase). Do not confuse it with 'Ihr' formal.

title: Demonstrativpronomen / Demonstratives
bridge: In Spanish, we use 'este/esta/estos/estas' to indicate proximity and 'ese/esa/esos/esas' for distance, and 'aquel/aquella' for something even farther. In German, the main distinction is between 'dies-' (near) and 'jen-' (far), but there's a catch: German doesn't have an exact equivalent of the intermediate 'ese'; 'dies-' is used for things nearby (even if they're a meter away) and 'jen-' for distant things. Another key difference: German demonstratives decline by gender, number, and case, just like articles, whereas in Spanish they only change by gender and number. Additionally, 'das' can be both a neutral article (the) and a demonstrative (that/this), which often confuses Spanish speakers.
rule: In German, the demonstratives are 'dieser' (this), 'diese' (this), 'dieses' (this/neuter) and 'diese' (these) for plural. For distance, 'jener' (that), 'jene' (that), 'jenes' (that/neuter) and 'jene' (those) are used. They decline like the definite article: in nominative, masculine 'dieser', feminine 'diese', neuter 'dieses', plural 'diese'. In accusative, masculine changes to 'diesen', feminine and neuter remain the same as nominative, plural 'diese'. In dative, masculine and neuter 'diesem', feminine 'dieser', plural 'diesen'. Special cases: 'das' can function as a neuter demonstrative (that/this) instead of 'dieses', and 'das' is also the neuter article. Typically, 'dieser' is used for something near the speaker, 'jener' for something far, and they are interchangeable in clear context.

concept_examples.translation: That house over there is very old.

common_error.explanation: The typical mistake is using 'este' as in Spanish without declining it, but in German the demonstrative must agree with the noun's gender. 'Haus' is neuter, so 'dieses' (or 'das') is used in nominative. Also, 'casa' in German is 'Haus' (neuter), not feminine. Remember: always use the correct form according to the noun's article (der/die/das).

examples.note: We use 'dieser' because 'Hund' is masculine.
'Blume' is feminine, so 'diese'.
'Buch' is neuter, so we use 'dieses'.
In accusative, masculine changes to 'diesen'.
Feminine does not change: 'diese'.
Neuter is the same as nominative: 'dieses'.

examples.translation: That tree over there is big.
examples.note: 'Jener' for distance with masculine noun.

examples.translation: That woman over there is my teacher.
examples.note: 'Jene' for feminine.
'Das' as a neuter demonstrative means 'that'.
'Das' in accusative, very common in conversation.

title: es gibt / There is (existence)
bridge: In Spanish, we use 'hay' for both singular and plural. In German, 'es gibt' (more formal) or 'da ist/da sind' (more colloquial) are used, which change depending on the number. Note: in German, 'es gibt' always takes the accusative case, while 'da ist' takes the nominative. Also, in negative sentences, we use 'kein' instead of 'no'.
rule: In German, to express existence, the main structures are 'es gibt' (there is/are) followed by the accusative, and 'da ist' (there is, singular) or 'da sind' (there are, plural) with the nominative. 'Es gibt' is invariable: it does not change for singular or plural. Examples: 'Es gibt ein Buch.' (There is a book.), 'Es gibt viele Bücher.' (There are many books.). To negate, use 'kein' (none) instead of 'nicht': 'Es gibt kein Buch.' (There is no book.). You can also use 'da ist' for singular and 'da sind' for plural: 'Da ist ein Tisch.' (There is a table.), 'Da sind Stühle.' (There are chairs.). In questions, the word order inverts: 'Gibt es ein Problem?' (Is there a problem?), 'Ist da ein Problem?' (Is there a problem?).

concept_examples.text: Da ist ein Hund im Garten.
concept_examples.translation: There is a dog in the garden.

concept_examples.text: Da sind zwei Katzen auf dem Sofa.
concept_examples.translation: There are two cats on the sofa.
concept_examples.phonetic: /daː zɪnt t͡svaɪ ˈkat͡sn̩ aʊf deːm ˈzoːfa/

concept_examples.text: Es gibt keine Milch im Kühlschrank.
concept_examples.translation: There is no milk in the fridge.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers often use 'nicht' to negate 'es gibt', but in German, to negate the existence of something, 'kein' (none) is used instead of 'nicht ein'. 'Nicht' is used to negate verbs or adjectives, but not indefinite nouns.

examples.note: Use 'es gibt' with accusative: 'ein Problem' (a problem).

examples.original: Es gibt viele Leute auf der Straße.
examples.phonetic: /ɛs ɡiːpt ˈfiːlə ˈlɔɪtə aʊf deːɐ̯ ˈʃtʁaːsə/
examples.translation: There are many people on the street.
examples.note: 'viele Leute' is in plural accusative (same as nominative).
'da ist' is more informal and used for singular.

examples.translation: There are flowers in the garden.
examples.note: 'da sind' for plural, with nominative.

examples.original: Da ist ein Auto vor dem Haus.
examples.phonetic: /daː ɪst aɪn ˈaʊ̯to foːɐ̯ deːm haʊ̯s/
examples.translation: There is a car in front of the house.
examples.note: The position of 'da' at the beginning is typical in German.
We use 'kein' before masculine/neuter nouns (accusative).

examples.translation: Is there a train station here?
examples.note: In questions, 'es gibt' inverts to 'gibt es'.

examples.original: Sind da Äpfel? - Nein, da sind keine.
examples.translation: Are there any apples? - No, there aren't any.
examples.note: In the answer, 'keine' is used to negate plural.

title: Präpositionen des Ortes / Prepositions of place
bridge: In Spanish, we use prepositions like 'en', 'sobre', 'debajo de' without changes to the noun. In German, prepositions of place require the article following them to change according to the case (dative or accusative), which can be confusing for Spanish speakers. The key is to ask: is there movement? If so, use accusative; if it's a static position, use dative. Additionally, many German prepositions have meanings that do not exactly match a single Spanish preposition, such as 'an' which can mean 'en' or 'junto a'.
rule: The most common prepositions of place in German are: 'in' (in, inside), 'an' (at, next to), 'auf' (on, on top of), 'über' (above, over, without contact), 'unter' (under), 'vor' (in front of), 'hinter' (behind), 'neben' (next to), 'zwischen' (between). These prepositions can govern either the dative case (position: wo? where?) or the accusative case (direction: wohin? where to?). In the dative case, the articles change: der→dem, die→der, das→dem. In the accusative case: der→den, die→die, das→das. For A1, we focus on the most common use (dative) and fixed contexts like 'nach Hause' (to home) or 'zu Hause' (at home). Exceptions: 'in' is used with countries and cities without an article, and 'nach' is used for directions without an article.

concept_examples.text: Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.
concept_examples.translation: The book is on the table.

concept_examples.text: Die Katze ist unter dem Bett.
concept_examples.translation: The cat is under the bed.
We are going to the cinema. (Literal: into the cinema)

common_error.wrong: Das Buch ist auf der Tisch.
common_error.correct: Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch.
common_error.correct_alt: Das Buch ist auf den Tisch. (if there is movement)
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish we say 'sobre la mesa' without changing the article. In German, with position prepositions (where), the dative case is used: der Tisch → dem Tisch. If it were movement (putting the book on the table), the accusative case would be used: den Tisch. Remember: after prepositions of place, ask 'wo?' (where) → dative, 'wohin?' (where to) → accusative.

levels.label: in, an, auf (en, junto a, sobre)

examples.note: 'in' is used with cities and countries without an article.

examples.original: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
examples.translation: The picture hangs on the wall.
examples.note: 'an' indicates vertical contact or proximity.

examples.original: Die Tasse ist auf dem Tisch.
examples.translation: The cup is on the table.
examples.note: 'auf' is used for horizontal surfaces with contact.

levels.label: über, unter, vor, hinter (sobre, debajo, delante, detrás)
levels.translation: above (without contact), under, in front of, behind

examples.original: Die Lampe hängt über dem Tisch.
examples.translation: The lamp hangs above the table (without touching it).
examples.note: 'über' is used for something higher than another thing without contact.

examples.original: Der Hund schläft unter dem Sofa.
examples.translation: The dog sleeps under the sofa.
examples.note: Remember that 'unter' requires the dative case in position.

examples.original: Das Auto steht vor dem Haus.
examples.translation: The car is in front of the house.
examples.note: 'vor' means in front of; in Spanish we sometimes use 'enfrente de'.

examples.original: Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.
examples.translation: The garden is behind the house.
examples.note: 'hinter' is the opposite of 'vor'.

levels.label: neben, zwischen, zu, nach (al lado de, entre, a, hacia)

examples.original: Die Bank ist neben dem Supermarkt.
examples.translation: The bank is next to the supermarket.
examples.note: 'neben' means next to; it is common in directions.

examples.original: Das Café ist zwischen der Kirche und dem Bahnhof.
examples.phonetic: [das kaˈfeː ɪst ˈtsvɪʃən deːɐ̯ ˈkɪʁçə ʊnt deːm ˈbaːnhoːf]
examples.translation: The café is between the church and the train station.
examples.note: 'zwischen' is used with two objects or places.

examples.translation: I am going to the party.
examples.note: 'zu' is used for direction towards a specific place (person or event).
'nach' is used with countries and cities without an article, and with cardinal directions.

title: Tage, Monate und Jahreszeiten / Days, months and seasons
bridge: In German, days, months, and seasons are always written with an initial capital letter, just like in Spanish, but unlike Spanish, most are masculine in gender and use the preposition 'am' (contraction of 'an dem') to indicate 'on' or 'the' (e.g., 'am Montag' = 'on Monday'). Additionally, in German, the date order is day, month, and year (as in Spanish), but the ordinal number is used with a period (1. Mai) and it is said as 'der erste Mai'. Note: months are not translated the same way; for example, 'März' in Spanish is 'March', not 'Tuesday'.
rule: In German, days of the week, months, and seasons are nouns and always start with a capital letter. The days of the week are: Montag (Monday), Dienstag (Tuesday), Mittwoch (Wednesday), Donnerstag (Thursday), Freitag (Friday), Samstag (Saturday), Sonntag (Sunday). The months are: Januar (January), Februar (February), März (March), April (April), Mai (May), Juni (June), Juli (July), August (August), September (September), Oktober (October), November (November), Dezember (December). The seasons are: Frühling (spring), Sommer (summer), Herbst (autumn), Winter (winter). To express 'in' with days, use 'am' (e.g., 'am Montag'), with months use 'im' (e.g., 'im Januar'), and with seasons also use 'im' (e.g., 'im Sommer'). For dates, the ordinal is used: the first of May = 'der erste Mai' or 'am ersten Mai'. Note: 'Samstag' is also called 'Sonnabend' in northern Germany, but 'Samstag' is more common. Exception: 'Mittwoch' does not contain 'tag' but is masculine.

concept_examples.translation: The first of January is New Year's Day.

common_error.explanation: A common mistake is to translate 'Hoy es lunes' literally into German as 'Heute ist Montag', but Spanish speakers sometimes say 'Hoy es lunes' in German as 'Heute ist der Montag' (with the article), which is incorrect in German. In German, no article is used when stating the day of the week in general. Say 'Heute ist Montag' without 'der'. Another correct variant is 'Heute haben wir Montag' (literally 'Today we have Monday'), which is more colloquial. Avoid the Spanish interference that sometimes uses 'el lunes'.

examples.note: Remember: all days end in '-tag' except 'Mittwoch'.
Literally means 'middle of the week'.
Also called 'Sonnabend' in northern Germany.
Used with 'am Sonntag' for 'on Sunday'.
Used with 'im Januar' for 'in January'.
Be careful with the umlaut, it is not 'Marz'.
Pronounced like 'mai' with a diphthong.
The shortest month with a 'z' pronounced as /ts/.
Used with 'im Frühling' for 'in spring'.
Same as in Spanish, but with the masculine article 'der'.
The 'h' is silent and 'st' is pronounced /ʃt/.
Written with 'W' that sounds like /v/.

title: Das Verb „haben“ / The verb 'to have'
bridge: In German, the verb 'haben' (to have) is an irregular verb that changes its stem in the 'du' and 'er/sie/es' forms. Unlike Spanish, where 'tener' is also irregular, in German the second person singular uses 'hast' instead of 'habst'. Additionally, in German the verb 'haben' is not used to express age (use 'sein' instead) nor to express sensations like hunger or thirst (use 'haben' with nouns, but be careful: you don't say 'tengo hambre' literally, but 'ich habe Hunger'). It is important to remember that 'haben' is always accompanied by an accusative case for the direct object.
rule:
The verb 'haben' (to have) is conjugated in the present indicative as follows:
- ich habe (I have)
- du hast (you have)
- er/sie/es hat (he/she/it has)
- wir haben (we have)
- ihr habt (you all have)
- sie/Sie haben (they/you formal have)

It is an irregular verb because the second and third person singular change the stem 'b' to 'st' and 't' respectively. It is used to express possession (Ich habe ein Buch), relationships (Ich habe einen Bruder), physical states (Ich habe Hunger), and with some verbs in the perfect tense. In German, age is expressed with 'sein' (Ich bin 20 Jahre alt), not with 'haben'. Additionally, 'haben' is used with the indefinite article 'ein/eine' and the definite article 'den/die/das' according to the accusative case.

common_error.explanation: In Spanish we say 'tengo 20 años', but in German age is expressed with the verb 'sein' (to be). Saying 'Ich habe 20 Jahre alt' is a literal translation that is incorrect. The correct form is 'Ich bin 20 Jahre alt'. You can also say 'Ich habe 20 Jahre' informally, but it is not the most common way.

examples.note: Remember that 'ein' is used for masculine and neuter, and 'eine' for feminine.
Notice the form 'hast' with 't' instead of 'b'. Also note 'einen' in the accusative masculine.
The third person singular is 'hat' without 'b'. 'Frage' is feminine, hence 'eine'.
The direct object is in the accusative: 'den Schlüssel' (the key).
The form 'ihr habt' is for the second person plural (you all).
The form 'sie' can mean 'they' or 'you', and 'Sie' (capitalized) is the formal form.
Literally 'I have hunger', but 'haben' + noun is used, not a verb.
Question with 'haben' in second person singular. 'Durst' means thirst.
Negation with 'kein' is used for nouns, here 'kein Geld'.

title: können / can (basic modal verb)
bridge: In Spanish, 'poder' is conjugated in the present tense as 'puedo, puedes, puede...'. In German, 'können' is also irregular: 'ich kann, du kannst, er kann'. Unlike Spanish, the modal verb in German goes in second position in main clauses, and the main verb is placed at the end in the infinitive. Additionally, in German, 'können' can express both ability ('know how to do something') and possibility ('it is possible'), just like 'poder' in Spanish, but be careful: to talk about 'knowing' (knowledge), 'kennen' (to know someone/something) or 'wissen' (to know facts) are used, while 'können' is only for skills. For example, 'Ich kann Deutsch sprechen' = 'I can speak German' (ability) and 'Das kann sein' = 'That can be' (possibility).
rule: The modal verb 'können' (can) is conjugated in the present tense as follows: ich kann, du kannst, er/sie/es kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie/Sie können. In a main clause, 'können' occupies the second position (or first if it's a question), and the main verb in the infinitive is placed at the end. For example: 'Ich kann gut schwimmen' (I can swim well). When used alone without another verb, 'können' means 'to know how to do something' (Ich kann das = I know how to do that). To express possibility, it is used with an infinitive or in impersonal constructions like 'Das kann sein' (That can be). It is commonly used to ask for permission politely (Kann ich bitte ...? = Can I ... please?). In questions, the order is inverted: 'Kannst du mir helfen?' (Can you help me?). Unlike Spanish, in German 'können' is not used to express 'can' as formal permission; in that case, 'dürfen' (more formal and permissive) is preferred. For A1 level, it is sufficient to know the forms for I, you (informal), he/she/it, we, you (plural informal), and they/you (formal).

common_error.explanation: In Spanish, we sometimes say 'puedo nadar' and the modal verb already includes the action, but in German, if you use 'können' with another verb, the second verb goes in the infinitive at the end, BUT you do not repeat 'können'. The common mistake Spanish speakers make is adding 'können' twice (like 'puedo poder nadar'). Only one modal verb is used. To express ability, you say 'Ich kann schwimmen' (I can swim). If you want to say 'I can do something else,' you use the main verb: 'Ich kann kochen' (I can cook).

examples.note: Notice that 'kann' has a short 'a' and no umlaut. Here it expresses ability.
The form 'kannst' for 'du' (you) is similar to Spanish, but remember the ending -st.
The third person singular 'kann' is the same as the first person, just like in Spanish 'puede'.
In questions, the modal verb comes first. In Spanish, intonation makes the question, but in German, it's the word order.
The negation 'nicht' is placed before the infinitive at the end. Be careful: in Spanish, 'no' comes before the verb.
For questions with 'er/sie/es,' the form is 'kann,' without 't.' Remember the inversion.
Here 'können' expresses possibility, not ability. It is equivalent to 'puede ser' in Spanish.

examples.original: Kann ich bitte die Rechnung haben?
examples.translation: Can I have the bill, please?
examples.note: Polite way to ask for something. Equivalent to 'Can I get the bill?'.
With 'Sie' (you formal/they), 'können' is used (same as 'they' and 'you' formal). Here it expresses permission.

title: Verbos irregulares básicos (gehen, kommen, tun, machen) / Basic irregular verbs
bridge: In Spanish, verbs like 'ir', 'venir', 'hacer' are also irregular, but in German you need to pay attention to vowel changes in the forms for 'du' and 'er/sie/es'. For example, 'gehen' (to go) changes to 'du gehst' and 'er geht', but the root remains the same. However, 'nehmen' (to take) changes from 'e' to 'i' in 'du nimmst'. Also, in German there is no distinction between 'ser' and 'estar' for these verbs, so 'gehen' is always 'to go' and has no direct equivalent in Spanish. Note: the verb 'tun' (to do) is used less than 'machen', but it is important for fixed expressions.
rule:
These four verbs are irregular in the present indicative. The forms are: 
- **gehen** (to go): ich gehe, du gehst, er/sie/es geht, wir gehen, ihr geht, sie/Sie gehen. The root does not change, only the ending. 
- **kommen** (to come): ich komme, du kommst, er/sie/es kommt, wir kommen, ihr kommt, sie/Sie kommen. No root change. 
- **tun** (to do/put): ich tue, du tust, er/sie/es tut, wir tun, ihr tut, sie/Sie tun. The vowel changes in du/er/sie/es (e -> u). 
- **machen** (to do/make): ich mache, du machst, er/sie/es macht, wir machen, ihr macht, sie/Sie machen. It is regular in the present, but is included because it is often confused with 'tun'. 
Typical uses: 
- 'gehen' is used for movement on foot: 'Ich gehe nach Hause' (I go home). 
- 'kommen' indicates coming or arriving: 'Er kommt morgen' (He is coming tomorrow). 
- 'tun' is used in expressions like 'Gutes tun' (to do good) or with pronouns: 'Was tust du?' (What are you doing?). 
- 'machen' is more common for activities: 'Ich mache Hausaufgaben' (I do homework). 
Do not use 'tun' for concrete actions as in the general Spanish 'hacer'; prefer 'machen'. Remember that in German the verb always goes in second position in declarative sentences.

concept_examples.text: Ich gehe jeden Tag zur Schule.
concept_examples.translation: I go to school every day.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈɡeːə ˈjeːdn̩ taːk tsuːɐ̯ ˈʃuːlə

concept_examples.translation: We are taking a break now.

common_error.explanation: The mistake is using the infinitive form 'machen' after 'ich'. In German, the verb must be conjugated according to the subject: 'ich' requires the ending '-e'. This error occurs because in Spanish the infinitive is sometimes used in colloquial constructions ('yo hacer los deberes') and due to influence from English ('I do'). To avoid it, memorize the conjugations and always check that the verb agrees with the subject in person and number.

examples.original: Ich gehe, du kommst, er macht
examples.phonetic: ɪç ˈɡeːə, duː kɔmst, eːɐ̯ maxt
examples.translation: I go, you come, he does/makes
examples.note: Observe the difference in endings: -e for ich, -st for du, -t for er.

examples.original: Wir tun, ihr tut, sie tun
examples.phonetic: vɪʁ tuːn, iːɐ̯ tuːt, ziː tuːn
examples.translation: We do, you all do, they do
examples.note: The verb 'tun' is irregular in du and er: 'tust' and 'tut'.
In questions, the conjugated verb comes before the subject.
For destinations, we use 'nach' with cities and countries without an article.
The imperative of 'kommen' for 'du' is 'komm' without an ending.
In German, we say 'einen Kaffee machen' instead of 'cocinar'.
Fixed expression with 'tun' that is not translated literally.
Use of 'machen' with abstract nouns; in Spanish we use 'tener'.

examples.translation: What do you do for a living?
examples.note: Common question to talk about professions.

title: Die Uhrzeit / Telling the time
bridge: In Spanish, to tell the time we use the verb 'ser' (es la una, son las dos) and hours are divided into 'y cuarto', 'y media', 'menos cuarto'. In German, the structure is different: 'Es ist' is used regardless of the number, and minutes are expressed differently, especially after the half hour (for example, 'halb drei' means 'two thirty', not 'three thirty' as it would be literally). Additionally, in German, the hour numbers are said first and then the minutes, but after 30 minutes, it indicates how many minutes are left until the next hour.
rule: In German, to tell the time at A1 level, the structure is: 'Es ist' + hour + 'Uhr' + (minutes). For exact hours: 'Es ist zwei Uhr' (It is two o'clock). For minutes from 1 to 24, the hour is said first followed by the minutes: 'Es ist zwei Uhr fünf' (It is five past two). For minutes from 25 to 59, the forms 'vor' (before) or 'nach' (past) are used with the next or current hour. After 30 minutes, 'halb' + next hour is commonly used (for example, 'halb drei' = two thirty). For 15 minutes, 'Viertel nach' (quarter past) or 'Viertel vor' (quarter to) is used. For exactly 30 minutes, 'halb' + next hour is used. For 45 minutes, 'Viertel vor' + next hour is used. Formal times (for example, in train schedules) use the 24-hour format and are said as 'vierzehn Uhr dreißig' (14:30). In colloquial speech, 'Uhr' can be omitted and 'Es ist zwei' is used.

common_error.explanation: A common mistake is to translate 'two thirty' literally as 'zwei Uhr halb', but in German the structure is 'halb' + next hour, without mentioning the current hour. Also, 'halb' always comes before the next hour. To avoid this error, remember that 'halb drei' means 'half of the third hour', i.e., two thirty. Alternatively, you can use the digital format 'zwei Uhr dreißig' (two thirty) to be clearer.

examples.note: 'Es ist' is used for all hours, unlike Spanish which changes between 'es' and 'son'.
'Uhr' is used to indicate exact hours.
Remember that in German there is no difference between 'es' and 'son'.
'Nach' is used for minutes past the hour, from 1 to 24.
'Viertel' means quarter of an hour.

levels.translation: Minutes before the next hour (from 31 to 59)

examples.note: 'Vor' is used to indicate minutes left until the next hour.
'Viertel vor' is used for 45 minutes.
You can also use the digital format: 'Es ist fünf Uhr vierzig'.
